text: Quick recap: an error budget is just one minus the SLO. At 99.9% availability over a 30-day window, the remaining 0.1% is roughly 43 minutes of allowed unavailability, spent by every SLI violation in that window. That mechanic hasn't changed. What changes at enterprise scale is what the organization actually does once that number is calculated — and that's what turns an error budget from a metric into a real decision-making tool.

The Google SRE book's central insight is that the error budget isn't meant to sit quietly on a dashboard. It's meant to be a negotiated agreement between product development and SRE about acceptable risk, decided in advance, before any incident forces the conversation. Without it, every reliability-versus-velocity argument becomes a fresh political fight in the moment. With it, the rule is already settled: as long as the budget isn't exhausted, product teams can ship and take reasonable risk, because the organization already agreed that level of risk was acceptable.

At enterprise scale, that agreement gets written down as an error budget policy — a real document, jointly owned by SRE and product leadership, spelling out the measurement window, the escalation path at warning thresholds, and, critically, what happens when the budget is fully exhausted. The well-documented consequence: the team stops shipping new features entirely and redirects its engineering capacity to reliability work until the budget recovers. In organizations that take this seriously, that's an enforced freeze, not a polite suggestion that quietly disappears under deadline pressure.

Not every bit of budget consumption deserves the same response, which is why mature practice distinguishes burn rate. A fast burn — budget consumed in hours because of an active outage — triggers an immediate page and incident response: stop the bleeding now. A slow burn — a service running a little worse than its SLO for days without any single dramatic incident — triggers a scheduled policy review instead, asking whether the team needs to pause and address systemic reliability debt. Alerting on burn rate, not raw error counts, is what lets an organization tell these two situations apart.

At one service, an exhausted budget is a conversation between two people. Across hundreds of services and dozens of teams, the written error budget policy is what lets that same decision get made consistently and fairly everywhere, without a VP personally adjudicating every feature freeze — real governance, not just a number. Next lesson turns to the other half of the Google SRE book's enforcement machinery: toil, and why reducing it gets real budget and headcount, not just good intentions.
